analysis.title: 2027 Global outlook - AI's next chapter
key_insights: AI remains the dominant investment story, but the debate has moved from the scale of the opportunity to its sustainability, as tech groups turn to cash and debt to fund data-centre build-outs. L&G's key takeaways: policy responses and energy constraints may dominate AI's next phase, higher-for-longer rates are becoming global, and decarbonisation holds the key to energy security.

L&G's Bubble Index covers five areas: credit expansion, macro conditions and disruptive change, speculative behaviour, valuations, and asset-price patterns. The first two flash warning signs. The other three suggest the market is not yet in bubble territory, since sentiment shows no widespread euphoria, most hyperscalers have de-rated and non-profitable tech has underperformed.

Global growth was resilient in 2026 despite an energy price surge, helped by AI investment spending. US real GDP growth is expected just above 2%, Europe at not much more than 1% because of its exposure to gas prices and limited fiscal support, and China is on track to hit its target. Consensus 2027 growth forecasts have changed little.

Growth risks are described as relatively balanced. Downside: further energy price rises feeding a broader inflation shock, the French presidential election (first round April 2027) amplifying sovereign debt concerns with spillover to the European periphery, and wider credit spreads from large AI debt issuance. Upside: resolution of the Strait of Hormuz disruption, renewed asset-price gains from AI productivity, and fewer central bank hikes than priced, especially in the UK.

L&G sees fewer rate hikes than priced as the most likely upside risk, because there is less pent-up demand than in 2022 and more labour market slack, which should limit second-round effects on wages and inflation.

AI's next phase may depend on energy supply, political support, geopolitical competition and financing. Power supply and transmission are a major bottleneck, local US opposition is raising project costs and timelines, and Democrat wins in key gubernatorial midterm races raise the prospect of political brakes on some data-centre development. Both parties still back the buildout to lead China.

Epoch AI estimates AI-driven computation volume has grown roughly five-million-fold since 2022, with an estimated 5.0M H100-equivalents of accelerator shipments in Q3 2026. Cloud demand makes up almost two-thirds of infrastructure demand and grows at a 23% CAGR, rising to 40%+ when AI demand is included. Infrastructure vacancy rates are at record lows.

On bubble risk, L&G cites BIS research that the boom could produce overcapacity as in the early 2000s. It argues today's infrastructure is mostly built to order, with data-centre development yields and cap rates stable (Green Street, Citi Research). An end would require supply to outstrip demand, and a correction would not invalidate the technology. Winners and losers will emerge within the AI ecosystem.

Portfolio view on AI: avoid treating it as a binary bet, separate exposure to adoption from exposure to current valuations, favour strong balance sheets and demonstrable revenue, and diversify across infrastructure providers and AI adopters. The eventual winners will not necessarily be the biggest spenders today.

US rates: the market priced about 50bps of easing for 2026 at the start of the year and now prices almost 100bps of hikes over 12 months. After September's 25bps hike, about 80bps more tightening is priced. L&G sees risks skewed toward less, with the cycle limited to reversing the 2025 insurance cuts, and has turned more constructive on the short and intermediate parts of the US curve.

Real yields account for more than 90% of the rise in US 10-year yields since the Iran war began, with inflation expectations up only modestly. L&G believes core inflation has probably peaked and notes consumers lack tax cuts or a high savings rate to cushion higher rates and energy prices.

France: the recent widening in French spreads came from higher global yields and debt-servicing costs, not a new political shock. The fiscal tightening needed to stabilise debt/GDP is exceptionally large. L&G has introduced French curve flatteners against Germany, reflecting a view that France may cap how far European yields can rise. Recent ECB communication is more dovish, which should temper European yield rises relative to others.

Emerging markets: the recent spread widening looks like a global rotation to quality rather than EM-specific deterioration. Market access is intact, FX reserves are near record levels and sovereign rating momentum is positive. L&G favours relative value over broad beta, around reform credibility, external buffers and looking beyond sovereign debt, and defines quality in fundamental terms, including some high-yield sovereigns.

Energy security: gas has shown exposure to severe price swings, and countries less dependent on gas, such as Spain, showed more resilience. L&G argues decarbonisation and electrification strengthen energy security, citing the European Commission's goal of raising electricity's share of final energy consumption from 23% to 46% by 2040. Investable areas include renewables, grids, storage, batteries and smart-grid technology, with the caveat that clean-energy supply chains are concentrated in China.

Defined contribution: the focus is shifting from accumulation to decumulation and retirement income, with sequencing risk, inflation and longevity central. Defined benefit: higher yields have improved funding, giving UK and US plans more endgame options (buyout, run-on, hibernation), and cashflow-driven investing and splitting liability and surplus portfolios are becoming more important. Tight corporate spreads limit the appeal of corporate bonds.

Surprise 1, US Treasury reckoning: L&G estimates the US must shrink its deficit by 5% of GDP over a decade to stabilise debt/GDP. Four episodes of that scale in major advanced economies in 45 years (Sweden, Canada, Italy, Spain). If it looks politically impossible, trouble could hit Treasuries, with alternative safe havens benefiting.

Surprise 2, growth asset rotation: AI capex relative to GDP (3-4% peak estimate for 2027E) rivals past booms. A rotation into lagging risk assets, benefiting non-US equities and mid-risk assets, could happen in a relatively benign way as earnings growth broadens.

Surprise 3, credit fragmentation: issuer dispersion has risen since the start of 2026 despite tight aggregate spreads (latest relative dispersion 0.479 on 16 October 2026). Dispersion is in the top quintile across Communications, Autos, Retailers and Financials ex-Banks, even excluding US hyperscalers. Surprise 4: investment-grade private credit pays a premium for complexity rather than credit risk. Surprise 5: real estate income resilience despite rate volatility.

Retail investors: participation has risen from about 8% of cash-equity volumes to peaks of 25-30%. Leveraged ETF assets reached a record $218B in 1H 2026, more than 4.5x the 2020 level. Equity holdings overtook housing as a share of US household wealth for the first time in 15 years. Retail crowding can make trend reversals sharp, and L&G points to big momentum swings in recent weeks.
L&G is rolling out a Global Toolkit for Investments (data, software and knowledge factories) to use AI in its own investment process.

sector_views.rationale: Demand exceeds supply, vacancy rates are at record lows and development yields and cap rates are stable, although power, politics and financing are constraints.
Decarbonisation and electrification support energy security, widening the opportunity from generation to storage, networks and flexibility.
Income creation in markets with tight supply and predictable demand offers resilience despite rate pressure.
Tight aggregate spreads offer little compensation for credit risk, but rising issuer dispersion favours security selection.

geopolitical: Middle East conflict and the Iran war raised energy prices and pushed up global yields.
Disruption in the Strait of Hormuz; resolution could rapidly reverse energy prices.
French presidential election, first round April 2027, amid sovereign debt concerns.
US-China competition in AI driving chip, data-centre, permitting and energy policy.
US midterms and Democrat gubernatorial wins raising prospects of political brakes on data-centre development.
Frontier AI models capable of orchestrating mass cyber-attacks and potentially designing novel pathogens or weapons.
Concentration of clean-energy supply chains in China (solar panels, batteries, power electronics).

tension_points.bull_case: Demand exceeds supply, infrastructure is built to order, vacancy is at record lows, and data-centre development yields and cap rates are stable. Hyperscalers have de-rated and sentiment is not euphoric.
tension_points.bear_case: BIS research suggests overcapacity as in the early 2000s, AI debt issuance is large, financing is tightening with higher rates, and power and political constraints are mounting.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Supply starting to outstrip demand, which L&G says would be required for the cycle to end.
